elementSpec.desc: describes the intellectual content of an object either as a series of paragraphs, summary or list of items.

objectIdentifier.objectName: The Adoration of the Mystic Lamb

objectContents.summary: The Ghent Altarpiece is a monumental 15th-century polyptych altarpiece consisting of 12 distinct physical oak panels, eight of which are double-sided wings. Together, they form an exhaustive and complex theological narrative visible in different configurations when open or closed. The work is believed to have been primarily created by Hubert van Eyck (d. 1426) and his brother Jan van Eyck (1441). It was unveiled on 6 May 1432.

objectItem.classCode: 71A51 Adam and/or Eve overcome with repentance
71A81 the sacrifice of Cain and Abel
objectItem.note: Recto: Adam, depicted with striking anatomical realism representing the fall of man. Above him is a small grisaille relief of Cain and Abel's sacrifices. Verso: The top inner-right shutter shows the Erythraean Sibyl and architectural detail below.

Recto: Singing Angels, displaying meticulously detailed facial expressions that reflect individual vocal ranges and pitches. Verso: The Annunciation (The Angel Gabriel), showing the archangel extending lilies while delivering his message to Mary. In a lunette above The Prophet Zechariah looks down.

objectItem.locus: Upper register, left-central fixed panel (recto only).
objectItem.note: The Virgin Mary enthroned as the Queen of Heaven, adorned with a crown of flowers and stars and reading a girdle book draped with a green cloth. This panel is covered from public view when the wings are closed.

objectItem.locus: Upper register, central fixed panel (recto only).
objectItem.classCode: 11C2 God the Father represented as human being
objectItem.note: The central Deity, interpreted as either God the Father or Christ in Majesty, or a unified representation of the Holy Trinity. He wears a crown similar to a papal tiara and deep red vestments, with an openwork earthly crown resting at his feet. This panel is covered from public view when the wings are closed.

objectItem.locus: Upper register, right-central fixed panel (recto only).
objectItem.note: Saint John the Baptist enthroned, wearing a green mantle over a cilice of camel hair. He is holding an open book on his lap, but pointing and looking across to the central Deity panel. This panel is covered from public view when the wings are closed.

Recto: Heavenly Musicians, depicting angels playing a pipe organ, harp, and viol, featuring Saint Cecilia at the keyboard. Verso: The Annunciation (The Virgin Annunciate). Her painted response to the angel ("Ecce ancilla Domini") is uniquely written upside down and backward so that God can read it from the heavens. In a lunette above the prophet Micah looks down.

objectItem.classCode: 71A51 Adam and/or Eve overcome with repentance
objectItem.note: Recto: Eve, in similar anatomical realism as Adam, holding a small citrus fruit (representing the forbidden fruit). Above her is a grisaille relief of Cain murdering Abel. Verso: The top inner-left shutter shows the Cumaean Sibyl looking down towards the Virgin. Below is architectural detail of the room for the annunciation scene.

Recto: The Just Judges, depicting secular rulers on horseback heading towards the central scene. Stolen in 1934, and never recovered, the object currently in the framework is a highly faithful 1945 copy painted by restorer Jef Van der Veken. Verso: A realistic donor portrait of Jodocus 'Joost' Vijd, the wealthy Ghent merchant who funded the altarpiece, shown kneeling in prayer.

Recto: The Knights of Christ (Christi Milites), displaying holy crusaders and armored warriors on horseback riding towards the adoration. Verso: A grisaille painting of Saint John the Baptist holding a lamb, looking slightly down towards the donor portrait for Joost Vijd.

objectItem.locus: Lower register, large central fixed panel (recto only).
objectItem.note: The core composition of the entire altarpiece. Depicts the Lamb of God bleeding into a chalice on a sacrificial altar, surrounded by angels. These are surrounded in a continuous landscape by (from the top-left anti-clockwise): the male martyrs, the pagan writers and Jewish prophets, the male saints, and the female martyrs.

objectItem.classCode: 11H(JOHN THE EVANGELIST) St John the Evangelist
objectItem.note: Recto: The Holy Hermits, portraying desert saints and ascetics (led by Anthony the Great, and including Mary Magdalene) navigating a rocky terrain towards the central panel of the adoration. Verso: A grisaille painting mimicking statue of Saint John the Evangelist holding a poisoned chalice, looking slightly down towards the portrait of Lysbette Borluut.

objectItem.classCode: 11H(CHRISTOPHER) The giant and martyr St Christopher
objectItem.note: Recto: The Holy Pilgrims, led by the giant Saint Christopher, walking through a lush Mediterranean landscape toward the adoration of the lamb. Verso: A vivid portrait of Lysbette Borluut, wife of Joost Vijd, shown kneeling in prayer.

physDesc.p: A massive polyptych that is 5.2m wide and up to 3.75m high composed of 12 oak panels painted in oil, housed in a complex, re-engineered structural framework that allows the hinged components to fold inward.

history.origin: The altarpiece is believed to have been created by Hubert van Eyck (d. 1426) and completed by his brother Jan van Eyck (d. 1441); unveiled on 6 May, 1432 inside the church of St. John the Baptist (now St. Bavo's Cathedral).
history.provenance: The work escaped Calvinist iconoclasts in 1566 when the altarpiece was dismantled and hidden the cathedral tower and later moved to the town hall. The panels were taken to Paris and exhibited at the Louvre after the French Revolution, being returned to Ghent in 1815 after the Battle of Waterloo. The Diocese of Ghent pawned them in 1815, and not repaying the debt they were sold to English collector Edward Solly who later sold them to Frederick William III (King of Prussia) who exhibited them in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin. These were later returned along with other panels which had been seized after World War I. During World War II they were taken by Nazi forces and eventually hidden in the Altaussee salt mines, and recovered by the Allied Monuments Men.
history.acquisition: The panels were returned to St. Bavo's Cathedral in Ghent, Belgium, in 1945, where the reassembled altarpiece remains in a climate-controlled, secure modern enclosure.

objectContents.summary: The UK Imperial State Crown (1937) is the crown worn by the British monarch during the State Opening of Parliament, and is a composite object which contains five historic stones whose individual histories are summarised below. The source of this information is the Royal Collections Trust.

objectItem.locus: Set into the front cross above the Cullinan II diamond.
objectItem.note: The Black Prince's Ruby, an irregular cabochon red spinel, whose documented history dates back to 14th-century Spain before being given to Edward, the Black Prince in 1367. It is believed that in 1415 it was one of the stones worn by Henry V in his helmet, at the Battle of Agincourt. The stone, which measures 170 carats, is of Eastern origin and has been drilled in the past for use as a pendant and this upper hole was later plugged with a small cabochon ruby in a gold slip mount.

objectItem.locus: Set into the front of the band, directly below the Black Prince's Ruby.
objectItem.note: The Cullinan II diamond (also known as the 'Lesser Star of Africa'), weighing 317.4 carats. It is the second-largest stone cut by the Asscher Diamond Company in 1908 from the massive 3,106-carat Cullinan diamond discovered in South Africa in 1905. The largest cleaving of the stone, Cullinan I, the Star of Africa, was placed in the Sovereign's Sceptre, and Cullinan II placed in the front of the band of the Imperial State Crown.

objectItem.locus: Set into the center of the cross pattée at the top of the crown.
objectItem.note: The St Edward's Sapphire, an octagonal rose-cut sapphire, is the oldest of the crown jewels thought to have been taken from the burial ring of Edward the Confessor (d. 1066). Legend has it that the King was asked for alms by a beggar, but having no money he gave the beggar a ring. The beggar supposedly later turned out to be St John the Evangelist, who when helping two English pilgrims in Syria since the King had helped him, asked that they return the ring to St Edward. The ring was on the King when he was buried, but in the 12th century they re-opened his tomb to retrieve the ring.

objectItem.locus: Set into the back of the bad opposite to the Cullinan II
objectItem.note: The Stuart Sapphire, is 104 carats and has been previously drilled for use as a pendant. It is believed to have been smuggled out of the country by James II when he fled in December 1688. James II passed it to his son, and it later became part of the collection of the Cardinal of York. After the Cardinal's death the sapphire was purchased for George IV. It was added to Queen Victoria's crown by the time of her coronation, and later moved to the rear of the crown in 1909

objectItem.locus: Suspended at the intersection of the arches
objectItem.note: The Queen Elizabeth's Earrings are four large pear-shaped pearls in rose-diamon caps. They are believed to be associated with the seven pearls that Pope Clement VII gave to Catherine de Medici when she married Henri II of France in 1533. While it is said that she then gave them to her daughter-in-law, Mary, Queen of Scots, and Elizabeth I bought them, more recent investigation shows that at least two of the pearls only entered the collection in the 19th century. It is unlikely, despite their name, that Elizabeth I ever wore them as earrings.

physDesc.p: The UK Imperial State Crown is formed from an openwork gold frame, mounted with three very large stones, and set with 2868 diamonds in silver mounts, largely table-, rose- and brilliant-cut, and a number of coloured stones in gold mounts, including 17 sapphires, 11 emeralds and 269 pearls. The crown weighs 1.06kg. The whole object measures 31.5 cm but 21.3 cm at the base of the object.

history.origin: Manufactured for the coronation of King George VI in 1937 by Garrard & Co., replacing the heavy 1838 frame built for Queen Victoria.
history.provenance: The crown was displayed at Garrards, Albemarle Street, prior to the coronation 4-6 May, 1937.
history.acquisition: Maintained in the Tower of London since its first use in George VI's coronation, with physical modifications made in 1953 to lower the arches for Queen Elizabeth II, and resized in 2023 for King Charles III. Vested in the Crown; held in trust for the nation by the Royal Collection Trust.

remarks.p: The objectContents element may be repeated where a single object itself contains multiple separate composite objects, or where these are considered an integral grouping they may be encoded with nested objectItem elements.
